title: Pharmacology of Cardiac Rhythm
subtitle: Week 02 · Lec 11 · Pharmacology of Cardiac Rhythm (Carrasco) | 20 questions

questions.text: If all Class I antiarrhythmic drugs block sodium channels, which of the following best explains why they are subdivided into three distinct families (IA, IB, and IC)?
options: Each subclass blocks a different phase of the cardiac action potential: Phase 0 for IA, Phase 2 for IB, and Phase 4 for IC
Each subclass targets a different receptor subtype on the sodium channel protein
The subclasses differ in which sodium channel states they preferentially bind, whether they also block potassium channels, and how quickly they dissociate from the channel
Each subclass selectively affects a different cardiac tissue: IA acts on atria, IB on ventricles, and IC on nodal tissue
questions.explanation:
Option C is correct: Class I subdivides because of three separate pharmacological axes — state-dependent binding, potassium channel co-blockade in IA, and wide variation in dissociation kinetics. Sodium channels cycle through resting, open (activated), and inactivated states; different Class I drugs have different affinity patterns across these states. Second, Class IA agents additionally block potassium channels, widening the action potential; Class IB and IC are more selective for sodium channels. Third, how rapidly a drug leaves the channel between beats varies from about 150 ms for lidocaine to 5 s for procainamide to 15–20 s for flecainide, and this kinetic difference drives the distinct ECG signatures of each family.
Option A is incorrect: Class I agents all decrease phase 0 depolarization; the subclass split is not based on which phase each drug targets.
Option B is incorrect: there are no distinct receptor subtypes on the sodium channel that map to IA, IB, or IC — the distinction is mechanistic (state preference and kinetics), not receptor-based.
Option D is incorrect: Class I agents are not tissue-selective in this way; lidocaine (IB), for example, is used for ventricular arrhythmias, not restricted to a single chamber.

questions.text: A pharmacologist studying sodium-channel binding kinetics compares three Class I antiarrhythmic agents at normal membrane potential. Which of the following correctly ranks their dissociation times from fastest to slowest?
options: Lidocaine (~150 ms) → Procainamide (~5 s) → Flecainide (~15–20 s)
Procainamide (~150 ms) → Lidocaine (~5 s) → Flecainide (~15–20 s)
Flecainide (~150 ms) → Lidocaine (~5 s) → Procainamide (~15–20 s)
Lidocaine (~150 ms) → Flecainide (~5 s) → Procainamide (~15–20 s)
questions.explanation:
Option A is correct: lidocaine (Class IB) dissociates in approximately 150 ms, procainamide (Class IA) in approximately 5 seconds, and flecainide (Class IC) in approximately 15–20 seconds. These quantified times define the three-family split: fast dissociation for IB, intermediate for IA, and slow for IC. Because Class IC blockade persists for many seconds between beats, even resting-rate QRS widening is expected with flecainide; procainamide accumulates progressively at faster heart rates; and lidocaine clears so rapidly that it barely widens the QRS in normal tissue. The kinetics are directly tied to use-dependence and the ECG effects tested in subsequent items.
Option B is incorrect: procainamide is not the fastest dissociating agent — that role belongs to lidocaine (150 ms).
Option C is incorrect: flecainide has the slowest dissociation (15–20 s), not the fastest, and its position with procainamide is reversed here.
Option D is incorrect: flecainide and procainamide are swapped — flecainide is the slow dissociator (IC), not procainamide.
Slide 11

questions.text: A patient with a structurally normal heart is started on a Class I antiarrhythmic drug. His follow-up ECG shows QRS duration of 90 ms, unchanged from his pre-treatment baseline of 88 ms. Which subclass of Class I drug is most consistent with this observation?
options: Class IA, because its intermediate dissociation permits complete channel recovery between beats in patients with normal hearts
Class IC, because it leaves action potential duration and ERP unchanged in Purkinje fibers and ventricles
Class IA, because its additional potassium channel blockade shortens repolarization, offsetting any tendency to widen the QRS
Class IB, because its rapid dissociation kinetics allow near-complete channel recovery between beats in a normal heart, producing little QRS widening
questions.explanation:
Option D is correct: Class IB agents such as lidocaine have rapid dissociation kinetics (~150 ms) that allow near-complete channel recovery during diastole in a normal heart, so they produce little or no QRS widening at resting heart rates. Because the sodium channel is largely unblocked by the time the next beat arrives, phase 0 conduction velocity is minimally affected. Class IA and IC drugs both have much slower dissociation times (5 s and 15–20 s, respectively), leaving residual blockade that slows phase 0 and widens the QRS even at normal rates. This is why lidocaine can suppress ectopy in ischemic tissue with minimal ECG change in normal myocardium.
Option A is incorrect: Class IA has intermediate kinetics (~5 s), which is far slower than one cardiac cycle at resting heart rates; substantial residual blockade persists and QRS widening is expected with Class IA.
Option B is incorrect: Class IC (flecainide, propafenone) is precisely the subclass that produces marked QRS widening; the unchanged APD and ERP in Purkinje fibers is a correct fact about IC, but it does not protect against QRS widening — conduction slowing from persistent Na+ blockade drives the QRS change.
Option C is incorrect: K+ channel co-blockade by Class IA prolongs APD and QT but does not shorten or negate QRS widening; Class IA widened both QRS and QT.
Slide 11

questions.text: A 67-year-old man with a myocardial infarction 2 weeks ago develops symptomatic ventricular tachycardia. He is started on IV lidocaine, which suppresses the arrhythmia. Experimental data have confirmed that lidocaine’s antiarrhythmic effect is stronger in ischemic tissue. Which of the following best explains this selectivity?
options: In ischemic tissue, lidocaine crosses the blood-brain barrier more readily and enhances central suppression of ectopic impulses
In depolarized ischemic tissue, lidocaine dissociates more slowly from sodium channels, substantially increasing the ERP in that tissue while leaving normal-tissue ERP relatively unaffected
Lidocaine preferentially binds resting-state sodium channels, which are more abundant in ischemic tissue due to incomplete repolarization
Lidocaine enhances outward potassium current in ischemic myocytes, shortening their action potential and eliminating the substrate for reentrant circuits
questions.explanation:
Option B is correct: at the more depolarized resting membrane potentials of ischemic tissue, lidocaine dissociates from sodium channels much more slowly (~0.5–1 s vs. ~150 ms in normal tissue), dramatically increasing the effective refractory period (ERP) selectively in ischemic myocardium. In normal tissue, lidocaine behaves as “fast in, fast out” — it blocks during depolarization but clears rapidly during diastole, leaving the ERP largely unaffected. In depolarized ischemic tissue, it becomes “fast in, slow out”: blockade accumulates and the ERP in the arrhythmogenic zone rises sharply, interrupting the reentrant circuit without substantially altering normal tissue excitability. This explains why lidocaine is a preferred agent for ischemic ventricular tachycardia after MI.
Option A is incorrect: lidocaine’s selectivity is a membrane-level kinetic phenomenon, not a CNS effect; the cardiac and CNS actions are separate and additive.
Option C is incorrect: lidocaine primarily binds open and inactivated (not resting) sodium channels; ischemic tissue traps lidocaine because slow dissociation prolongs channel occupancy, not because resting-state channels are more abundant.
Option D is incorrect: lidocaine does not enhance outward potassium current; its mechanism is purely sodium channel blockade.

questions.text: A 58-year-old woman is started on quinidine for rhythm control of chronic atrial fibrillation. Three weeks later she reports ringing in her ears, blurred vision, and intermittent headaches. Her ECG is ordered. Which of the following additional risks of quinidine is most important to discuss given these new symptoms?
options: Lupus-like syndrome requiring anti-nuclear antibody monitoring
Pulmonary fibrosis requiring annual pulmonary function testing
Progressive QT shortening leading to accelerated idioventricular rhythm
QT prolongation with risk of torsades de pointes and increased overall mortality
questions.explanation:
Option D is correct: the symptoms — tinnitus, blurred vision, and headache — constitute cinchonism, a syndrome from quinidine’s origin in the cinchona tree, and this presentation coincides with quinidine’s risk of prolonged QT with torsades de pointes and increased mortality. Quinidine (Class IA) blocks both sodium and potassium channels. K+ blockade lengthens the QT interval and predisposes to torsades de pointes; quinidine is one of the few antiarrhythmics shown to increase all-cause mortality despite maintaining sinus rhythm. The full cinchonism syndrome includes blurred vision, tinnitus, headache, and psychosis at higher doses.
Option A is incorrect: lupus-like syndrome and ANA monitoring are specific to procainamide (also Class IA), not quinidine; these two drugs have distinct adverse-effect profiles despite sharing the IA subclass.
Option B is incorrect: pulmonary fibrosis and PFT monitoring are adverse effects of amiodarone (Class III/IV/I/II), not quinidine.
Option C is incorrect: quinidine prolongs the QT interval via K+ channel blockade (shared IA mechanism); it does not shorten QT. Class IB agents (lidocaine, mexiletine) produce a slight QT decrease.
Slide 15 · Transcript 35:31

questions.text: A 54-year-old man is receiving IV lidocaine for ischemic ventricular tachycardia in the coronary care unit. His nurse calls to report that he is now experiencing vivid visual hallucinations and coarse tremors of both hands. His serum lidocaine level is at the upper end of the therapeutic range. Which of the following best explains the new findings?
options: Cinchonism from cross-reactivity with quinidine’s cinchona alkaloid pathway
Serum-sickness–type hypersensitivity reaction to a lidocaine metabolite
CNS toxicity from sodium channel blockade, manifesting as tremor, ataxia, and hallucinations
Drug-induced lupus activating antinuclear antibodies that cross-react with CNS tissue
questions.explanation:
Option C is correct: at high or upper-therapeutic lidocaine levels, sodium channel blockade in the CNS produces a characteristic toxicity syndrome including tremor, ataxia, and hallucinations. Neuronal sodium channels are equally susceptible to lidocaine’s blocking action; the CNS manifestations precede and predict cardiac toxicity at rising serum levels. Dose-dependent cardiovascular effects (bradycardia, heart block) can also emerge at toxic levels. Monitoring for these neurological warning signs is part of safe IV lidocaine administration.
Option A is incorrect: cinchonism (tinnitus, blurred vision, headache, psychosis) is specific to quinidine’s cinchona-tree origin; lidocaine is a synthetic aminoamide with no structural or mechanistic relationship to quinine.
Option B is incorrect: hypersensitivity or serum-sickness reactions are not the recognized dose-related toxicity profile of lidocaine; these would not present with the neurological toxidrome described.
Option D is incorrect: drug-induced lupus is a specific adverse effect of procainamide (Class IA), diagnosed by positive ANA. Lidocaine does not cause lupus-like syndrome.
Slide 15 · Transcript 34:57

questions.text: A 63-year-old man with known coronary artery disease (prior NSTEMI, EF 55%) presents with recurrent paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. He has no structural cardiomyopathy or heart failure. Based on landmark clinical trial evidence, which of the following antiarrhythmics should be avoided in this patient?
options: Flecainide, which was shown to increase the risk of death in patients with coronary artery disease in the CAST trial
Ibutilide, which is safe only in structurally normal hearts and is contraindicated following myocardial infarction
Dofetilide, which requires inpatient ECG monitoring and is not used in patients with prior ischemic events
Sotalol, which is specifically contraindicated in patients with any degree of coronary artery disease
questions.explanation:
Option A is correct: flecainide (Class IC) is contraindicated in patients with coronary artery disease because the CAST trial demonstrated a significantly increased risk of death compared to placebo, despite effective arrhythmia suppression. Flecainide’s indication is atrial fibrillation in patients with structurally normal hearts. In the presence of structural or ischemic heart disease — including cardiomyopathy, congenital disease, or CAD — Class IC agents must not be used. The CAST trial remains a landmark warning about the hazard of assuming arrhythmia suppression translates to mortality benefit.
Option B is incorrect: ibutilide is a Class III agent used for acute pharmacologic cardioversion in appropriate patients; while it is not typically used for long-term maintenance, its contraindication profile is not specifically post-MI CAD.
Option C is incorrect: dofetilide does require continuous ECG monitoring due to QT prolongation risk, but it is not specifically avoided in all ischemic patients — it is used for AF/flutter maintenance; the specific CAD mortality risk from landmark trial data is flecainide’s distinction.
Option D is incorrect: sotalol has dual Class II and Class III properties and is used for maintenance of sinus rhythm and ventricular tachycardia; it is not categorically contraindicated in all CAD, though it is used cautiously. The CAST trial finding is unique to Class IC agents.
Slide 15 · Transcript 34:06

questions.text: During a graded exercise test, a healthy patient’s heart rate increases from 65 to 148 beats per minute. Which of the following best describes the cellular mechanism by which endogenous norepinephrine increases the SA node firing rate?
options: Norepinephrine activates adenosine A1 receptors on SA nodal cells, hyperpolarizing them and paradoxically shortening the time between beats
Norepinephrine increases Iₑ (funny current) and slow inward Ca²⁺ current, steepening the slope of phase 4 depolarization and shortening the time to threshold
Norepinephrine directly inhibits Iᴷr channels in SA nodal cells, prolonging phase 3 repolarization and increasing automaticity
Norepinephrine activates M2 muscarinic receptors on SA nodal cells, increasing the conductance of inwardly rectifying K⁺ channels
questions.explanation:
Option B is correct: norepinephrine (via beta-adrenergic receptors) increases the funny current (Iₑ) and the slow inward calcium current in SA nodal cells, which steepens the slope of phase 4 depolarization so that threshold is reached sooner and the firing rate increases. Beta-adrenergic stimulation raises cAMP, which shifts the activation voltage of HCN channels (responsible for Iₑ) to more positive values, making them open earlier in diastole. Simultaneously, increased Ca²⁺ influx accelerates the membrane reaching threshold. This is the direct converse of beta-blocker action: blocking these currents (Class II mechanism) slows the heart. Understanding NE’s mechanism anchors why beta-blockers are effective antiarrhythmics.
Option A is incorrect: adenosine A1 receptor activation produces the opposite effect to norepinephrine — it hyperpolarizes SA nodal cells (via GIRK K⁺ channels) and slows the heart rate; NE acts on beta-adrenergic, not adenosine, receptors.
Option C is incorrect: Iᴷr block would prolong repolarization and could reduce rather than increase automaticity; IKr channel inhibition is the mechanism of Class III drugs, not catecholamines.
Option D is incorrect: M2 muscarinic receptor activation is the parasympathetic (vagal) mechanism — it reduces heart rate; NE acts on adrenergic receptors, which is the sympathetic pathway.
Slide 17 · Transcript 37:55

questions.text: A 48-year-old man with essential hypertension has taken metoprolol 100 mg daily for three years with excellent rate control. He runs out of his prescription and goes 4 days without the medication before presenting to urgent care with blood pressure 178/104 mm Hg and heart rate 118 beats per minute. Which of the following best explains his current presentation?
options: Rebound increase in vagal tone causing paradoxical tachycardia after beta receptor downregulation
Unopposed norepinephrine effect exclusively on beta-2 receptors in the SA node, bypassing beta-1–mediated rate control
Beta blocker withdrawal syndrome: upregulation of beta-adrenergic receptors during chronic blockade leaves them unmasked on abrupt cessation, causing rebound tachycardia and hypertension
Loss of Class II antiarrhythmic effect unmasking a latent supraventricular tachycardia requiring ablation
questions.explanation:
Option C is correct: abrupt cessation of a beta blocker causes withdrawal syndrome characterized by rebound tachycardia and hypertension, driven by upregulation of beta-adrenergic receptors during chronic blockade. With chronic beta-blocker use, the body upregulates receptor density as a compensatory response. When the drug is suddenly stopped, the now-abundant receptors are exposed to normal circulating catecholamines, producing an exaggerated adrenergic response: sinus tachycardia and hypertensive rebound. This is listed among the cardiac adverse effects of beta blockers on slide 19 and underscores the need for gradual tapering when discontinuing.
Option A is incorrect: vagal tone does not “rebound” with cessation of a sympatholytic drug; the mechanism is adrenergic receptor upregulation, not parasympathetic activation.
Option B is incorrect: beta-1 receptors (heart rate, inotropy) are the primary cardiac targets; beta-2 receptors at the SA node are a minor contributor, and the distinction does not explain the syndrome.
Option D is incorrect: a latent SVT is a distinct clinical entity requiring its own workup; the temporal relationship to medication cessation and the combination of tachycardia with marked hypertension strongly favors withdrawal syndrome rather than a primary arrhythmia.
Slide 19

questions.text: A 51-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and recurrent SVT is prescribed propranolol. His wife reports that last week he became confused and diaphoretic without the rapid heartbeat he normally notices when his glucose drops. A fingerstick at home read 48 mg/dL. Which adverse effect of propranolol MOST directly explains the absence of palpitations?
options: Propranolol’s alpha-blocking activity blunts the peripheral vasoconstrictive response to hypoglycemia, masking reflex tachycardia
Propranolol reduces insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells, blunting the counter-regulatory response to low glucose
Propranolol’s negative inotropic effect prevents the compensatory increase in cardiac output that would otherwise generate palpitations
Beta-2 receptor blockade by propranolol prevents epinephrine-mediated tachycardia, eliminating the warning sign that normally alerts this patient to hypoglycemia
questions.explanation:
Option D is correct: propranolol is non-selective, blocking both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors; beta-2 blockade specifically prevents the epinephrine-mediated tachycardia that normally serves as a warning symptom of hypoglycemia in diabetic patients. During hypoglycemia, epinephrine is released as a counter-regulatory hormone. Beta-2 stimulation by epinephrine produces tachycardia (and tremor); propranolol’s beta-2 blockade suppresses this adrenergic warning signal. The patient remains diaphoretic — a cholinergic response not blocked by propranolol — but loses the palpitations that serve as his usual cue to check glucose. Beta-1 selective agents (metoprolol, esmolol) are preferred in diabetic patients prone to hypoglycemia for exactly this reason.
Option A is incorrect: propranolol does not have alpha-blocking properties; that profile belongs to carvedilol (alpha + beta blocker). Propranolol’s relevant receptor blockade is beta-1 and beta-2.
Option B is incorrect: propranolol can impair glycogenolysis (a beta-2 effect) and may modestly reduce insulin secretion, but these metabolic effects are distinct from the warning-symptom masking mechanism.
Option C is incorrect: negative inotropy reduces stroke volume but does not specifically eliminate palpitations as a hypoglycemic warning sign; the tachycardia signal, not contractility per se, is what the patient notices.
Slide 19 · Transcript 40:47

questions.text: A hospitalized patient in continuous atrial fibrillation for 30 hours requires pharmacologic management. The electrophysiologist selects Drug X for immediate IV administration to restore sinus rhythm, then prescribes Drug Y orally to prevent recurrence after cardioversion succeeds. Which of the following correctly identifies Drug X and Drug Y?
options: Drug X = dofetilide; Drug Y = ibutilide
Drug X = ibutilide; Drug Y = dofetilide
Drug X = sotalol; Drug Y = ibutilide
Drug X = ibutilide; Drug Y = sotalol, because sotalol simultaneously cardioverts and maintains sinus rhythm
questions.explanation:
Option B is correct: ibutilide (Class III) is indicated for acute pharmacologic cardioversion of atrial fibrillation, while dofetilide is indicated for maintenance of sinus rhythm after cardioversion. Ibutilide is given intravenously and can restore sinus rhythm within minutes to hours. Dofetilide is an oral agent used to keep patients in sinus rhythm after cardioversion of AF or atrial flutter. These two drugs cover the two phases: ibutilide converts, dofetilide maintains.
Option A is incorrect: the roles of dofetilide and ibutilide are reversed; dofetilide maintains but does not acutely cardiovert, and ibutilide converts but is not used for long-term maintenance.
Option C is incorrect: sotalol does not convert atrial fibrillation — it is explicitly not a cardioverting agent; using sotalol as Drug X would be inappropriate for this acute role.
Option D is incorrect: the premise “sotalol simultaneously cardioverts and maintains” is false. Sotalol maintains sinus rhythm after cardioversion has been achieved by other means; it does not itself convert AF. Ibutilide is correctly identified as Drug X, but Drug Y should be dofetilide, not sotalol.
Slide 21 · Transcript 42:13

questions.text: An electrophysiology fellow is reviewing Class III antiarrhythmic options with a senior attending. Regarding sotalol, which of the following statements is MOST accurate?
options: Sotalol maintains sinus rhythm after cardioversion of AF or flutter and treats sustained VT, but it does not convert AF to sinus rhythm
Sotalol can restore sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation when given intravenously, making it the preferred agent for acute pharmacologic cardioversion
Sotalol’s purely Class III mechanism distinguishes it from ibutilide, which additionally blocks beta-adrenergic receptors
Sotalol is indicated for acute pharmacologic cardioversion of atrial flutter but must not be used in atrial fibrillation due to its beta-blocking properties
questions.explanation:
Option A is correct: sotalol maintains sinus rhythm after cardioversion of AF or atrial flutter and treats sustained ventricular tachycardia, but it is explicitly not a cardioverting agent and does not convert atrial fibrillation to sinus rhythm. This distinction is clinically important: a physician planning rhythm control for a patient in AF cannot use sotalol alone — cardioversion must be achieved first (electrically or with an appropriate agent such as ibutilide), and sotalol is then used to prevent recurrence. Sotalol also has beta-blocking (Class II) properties in addition to its Class III IKr blockade, making it a racemic mixture with dual receptor activity.
Option B is incorrect: sotalol is explicitly not a cardioverting agent and does not convert AF; IV cardioversion is not a sotalol indication.
Option C is incorrect: the description of mechanisms is reversed — sotalol has both Class III (IKr blockade) and Class II (beta-1/beta-2 blockade) activity; ibutilide is a more selective IKr blocker without beta-blocking properties.
Option D is incorrect: sotalol is used for both atrial flutter and atrial fibrillation (for maintenance), not restricted to flutter; and its beta-blocking properties are a feature of its mechanism, not a contraindication to its AF use.
Slide 22

questions.text: A cardiologist plans to transition a patient from amiodarone to dronedarone after a period of rhythm stability. She warns the patient that careful washout planning will be needed because of amiodarone’s pharmacokinetics. Which of the following MOST accurately describes the half-lives of amiodarone and dronedarone?
options: Amiodarone: approximately 24 hours; Dronedarone: approximately 25–70 days
Amiodarone: approximately 9 minutes; Dronedarone: approximately 24 hours
Both amiodarone and dronedarone have half-lives in the 24–48 hour range, allowing safe transition within a few days
Amiodarone: 25–70 days; Dronedarone: approximately 24 hours
questions.explanation:
Option D is correct: amiodarone has a half-life of 25–70 days, while dronedarone’s half-life is approximately 24 hours. This order-of-magnitude difference has major clinical consequences. Amiodarone’s extreme lipophilicity leads to massive tissue accumulation (heart, lung, liver, cornea), and its multi-week washout means that drug interactions and toxicities can persist long after discontinuation. Dronedarone was developed in part to offer a shorter-acting alternative with a more manageable adverse-effect profile. The half-life contrast also explains why overlapping coverage and loading strategies differ substantially between the two agents.
Option A is incorrect: the half-lives are reversed; 24 hours is dronedarone’s half-life and 25–70 days is amiodarone’s.
Option B is incorrect: a 9-minute half-life describes esmolol (Class II, IV only), not amiodarone; amiodarone’s half-life is measured in weeks, not minutes.
Option C is incorrect: amiodarone’s half-life (25–70 days) and dronedarone’s (~24 hours) are not in the same range; confusing them has clinical consequences for transition planning and drug interaction management.
Slide 23

questions.text: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation and a mechanical heart valve is maintained on warfarin with a stable INR of 2.3. His cardiologist starts amiodarone for recurrent ventricular tachycardia. Three weeks later his INR is 5.2 and he reports easy bruising. Which of the following best explains the drug interaction and the appropriate dose adjustment?
options: Amiodarone displaces warfarin from albumin binding sites, increasing free warfarin; the warfarin dose should be reduced by 25%
Amiodarone induces CYP2C9, increasing warfarin clearance; the warfarin dose should be increased to maintain therapeutic anticoagulation
Amiodarone inhibits CYP450 enzymes responsible for warfarin metabolism, increasing warfarin exposure; the warfarin dose should be reduced by approximately 50%
Amiodarone’s iodine-mediated thyroid toxicity decreases vitamin K–dependent clotting factor synthesis, requiring warfarin to be discontinued
questions.explanation:
Option C is correct: amiodarone is a potent CYP450 inhibitor that impairs warfarin’s hepatic metabolism, causing warfarin levels to rise; the standard recommendation is to reduce the warfarin dose by approximately 50% when amiodarone is initiated. Amiodarone inhibits multiple CYP450 isoforms (including CYP2C9 and CYP3A4), slowing the clearance of drugs metabolized by these pathways. Warfarin’s S-enantiomer is primarily CYP2C9-dependent; inhibition raises its plasma concentration, prolonging the INR. The interaction can persist for weeks after amiodarone is started or stopped, given amiodarone’s 25–70–day half-life. Digoxin levels are similarly affected and should also be reduced by approximately 50%.
Option A is incorrect: plasma protein displacement is not the primary mechanism; CYP450 inhibition is. A 25% reduction is also insufficient — the slide specifies a 50% dose reduction.
Option B is incorrect: amiodarone inhibits (does not induce) CYP450 enzymes; induction would speed warfarin clearance and lower the INR, the opposite of what is observed here.
Option D is incorrect: while amiodarone can cause thyroid dysfunction due to its iodine content, the acute warfarin-INR interaction is a CYP450 drug-drug interaction, not a clotting-factor synthesis effect; warfarin is continued with dose adjustment, not discontinued.
Slide 24 · Transcript 47:43

questions.text: A 65-year-old woman with symptomatic heart failure (EF 28%), persistent atrial fibrillation, and no prior life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia requires long-term rhythm control. Her cardiologist considers amiodarone versus dronedarone. Which of the following CORRECTLY describes their relative use in this clinical scenario?
options: Dronedarone is preferred because it lacks iodine and therefore avoids thyroid toxicity, which is particularly dangerous in patients with heart failure
Amiodarone is appropriate here; dronedarone carries a black box warning against use in patients with heart failure based on the Andromeda trial
Dronedarone is preferred because its 24-hour half-life allows safer dose titration in patients with reduced ejection fraction
Both agents are equally contraindicated in symptomatic heart failure because their shared multi-class antiarrhythmic properties worsen myocardial depression
questions.explanation:
Option B is correct: dronedarone carries a black box warning against use in symptomatic heart failure; this warning originated from the Andromeda trial meta-analysis, which showed increased mortality in CHF patients on dronedarone. Amiodarone is actually considered safer in patients with CHF and post-MI. Dronedarone’s structural similarity to amiodarone (minus the iodine atoms) was intended to reduce organ toxicity, but the Andromeda data revealed it could worsen outcomes in heart failure. Amiodarone, despite its extensive toxicity profile in other organs, has not shown the same CHF mortality signal and can be used when other options are unsuitable in patients with reduced EF. The clinical rule is clear: dronedarone is for patients with preserved cardiac function.
Option A is incorrect: while the absence of iodine reduces dronedarone’s thyroid burden, this benefit does not override the black box warning against CHF use; thyroid toxicity avoidance is irrelevant if the drug increases mortality in this population.
Option C is incorrect: dronedarone’s shorter half-life is a pharmacokinetic advantage in general but does not make it safer in patients with heart failure; the Andromeda black box applies regardless of half-life.
Option D is incorrect: amiodarone is not equally contraindicated in CHF — it is specifically listed as safer in CHF and post-MI, distinguishing it from dronedarone in this regard.
Slide 24 · Transcript 48:02

questions.text: A patient is recovering from an anterior STEMI. The intern notes the patient’s resting heart rate is 92 beats per minute and asks whether adding a calcium channel blocker would help reduce long-term mortality, as it would with a beta blocker. Which of the following BEST represents the established role of calcium channel blockers in post-MI management?
options: Calcium channel blockers do not reduce mortality after myocardial infarction and should not be added for that indication
Non-DHP calcium channel blockers reduce post-MI mortality by approximately 25% when combined with aspirin and beta-blocker therapy
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers reduce infarct size and 30-day mortality when started within 12 hours of STEMI
All calcium channel blockers reduce post-MI mortality by lowering myocardial oxygen demand, making them first-line secondary prevention agents
questions.explanation:
Option A is correct: calcium channel blockers do not reduce mortality after myocardial infarction, and this is an explicit negative teaching point from the lecture. Unlike beta-blockers — which have well-established mortality benefit post-MI through multiple mechanisms — calcium channel blockers lack this outcome data. In fact, non-DHP agents (verapamil, diltiazem) reduce contractility and can worsen outcomes in patients with depressed systolic function (the major adverse consequence of Class IV agents is myocardial depression, and they must be used cautiously in heart failure). Rate slowing with a CCB is not a substitute for beta-blocker therapy in the post-MI setting.
Option B is incorrect: no landmark trial demonstrates a 25% mortality reduction with non-DHP CCBs post-MI; this figure and the claimed combination benefit are fabricated. The slide explicitly states CCBs do NOT reduce mortality after MI.
Option C is incorrect: dihydropyridine CCBs act on vascular smooth muscle, not cardiac nodal tissue; they are not antiarrhythmics (Class IV) and have no established role in reducing post-MI mortality.
Option D is incorrect: this statement directly contradicts the lecture’s explicit negative finding; CCBs are not first-line secondary prevention agents post-MI.
Slide 27

questions.text: A patient with atrial flutter is started on verapamil for rate control. Which of the following cardiac effects is MOST directly produced by verapamil’s blockade of L-type calcium channels in AV nodal tissue?
options: Decreased AV nodal effective refractory period (ERP), allowing faster conduction of flutter impulses to the ventricles
Increased automaticity in the SA node, producing a stable pacemaker that competes with and suppresses the flutter focus
Increased AV nodal effective refractory period (ERP), reducing the number of flutter impulses conducted to the ventricles and slowing the ventricular rate
Decreased myocardial contractility only, with no direct effect on AV nodal conduction or refractoriness
questions.explanation:
Option C is correct: verapamil (Class IV) increases the AV nodal effective refractory period (ERP) by blocking L-type calcium channels, which are responsible for phase 0 depolarization in AV nodal tissue; this directly slows conduction of atrial impulses to the ventricles. Because AV nodal phase 0 depends on slow inward Ca²⁺ current (not fast Na⁺ current as in working myocardium), L-type channel blockade lengthens the time the node requires to recover before it can conduct the next impulse. In atrial flutter, this means fewer flutter waves are transmitted to the ventricles, lowering the ventricular rate. The authoritative slide (slide 26) explicitly lists “Increase the AV nodal effective refractory period (ERP)” among verapamil’s cardiac effects.
Option A is incorrect: a decreased AV nodal ERP would increase conduction of flutter impulses and accelerate the ventricular rate — the opposite of verapamil’s therapeutic goal. This is a known typo in one summary table; the authoritative mechanism (slide 26) is ERP increase.
Option B is incorrect: verapamil decreases SA nodal automaticity; it is a negative chronotrope. It does not enhance pacemaker activity or compete with ectopic foci through automaticity.
Option D is incorrect: verapamil does decrease myocardial contractility (a clinically important adverse effect, particularly with verapamil), but it also has direct and well-established effects on AV nodal conduction and refractoriness that are the basis for its antiarrhythmic use.

questions.text: A patient with new-onset ventricular tachycardia has a ventricular rate of 210 beats per minute. The emergency physician is choosing among Class I antiarrhythmic subclasses. Based on use-dependence, which subclass would produce the GREATEST increase in QRS duration at this rapid rate compared to the same drug at a resting rate of 65 beats per minute?
options: Class IA, because its additional potassium channel blockade amplifies sodium channel effects at rapid rates
Class IB, because its fast dissociation kinetics shift to a slow-dissociation pattern exclusively in tachycardic tissue
Class IA and IB equally, because both are sodium channel blockers and share the same use-dependence mechanism
Class IC, because its slow dissociation kinetics cause the greatest accumulation of residual sodium channel blockade as diastolic intervals shorten at high heart rates
questions.explanation:
Option D is correct: Class IC shows the highest use-dependence because its slow dissociation kinetics (~15–20 s for flecainide) mean that residual blockade accumulates dramatically as the diastolic interval shrinks at fast heart rates, producing progressively greater QRS widening. At a ventricular rate of 210 bpm, diastolic intervals fall to less than 200 ms — far shorter than flecainide’s 15–20 s dissociation time. Blockade builds with each successive beat, widening the QRS far beyond what is seen at rest. Class IA has intermediate use-dependence (dissociation ~5 s), and Class IB has the least or absent use-dependence (dissociation ~150 ms, clearing almost entirely between beats even at fast rates). The use-dependence rank order is: IC (highest) → IA (intermediate) → IB (lowest).
Option A is incorrect: Class IA’s K+ channel co-blockade is the reason for its QRS plus QT effect, not the driver of its use-dependence; the use-dependence magnitude for IA is intermediate, not the greatest.
Option B is incorrect: Class IB dissociates rapidly (~150 ms) at normal membrane potentials; in ischemic/depolarized tissue it dissociates more slowly, but this tissue-level kinetic change is distinct from use-dependence and does not make IB the most use-dependent subclass.
Option C is incorrect: Class IA and IB do not share equal use-dependence; the slide explicitly shows IA as intermediate, IB as absent/no use-dependence, and IC as highly use-dependent.

questions.text: A 50-year-old woman with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and a structurally normal heart is started on flecainide. On a follow-up ECG one week later, her QRS duration is 115 ms, compared to a pre-treatment baseline of 88 ms. She has a resting heart rate of 64 beats per minute. Which of the following BEST explains the QRS widening even at rest?
options: Flecainide’s slow dissociation kinetics cause substantial sodium channel blockade to persist between beats even after membrane repolarization, producing marked QRS widening at any heart rate
Flecainide’s additional potassium channel blockade prolongs phase 3 repolarization, which indirectly widens the QRS by extending the time the myocardium is refractory
Flecainide preferentially blocks sodium channels in the resting state, causing cumulative blockade specifically in structurally abnormal myocardium
Flecainide widens the QRS only at elevated heart rates via use-dependence; baseline QRS widening of this magnitude indicates a toxic serum level requiring dose reduction
questions.explanation:
Option A is correct: flecainide’s dissociation time of 15–20 seconds is far longer than any physiologic cardiac cycle, so substantial blockade persists between every beat even at slow resting heart rates, producing marked QRS widening that is present from initiation of therapy. Unlike Class IB agents that clear between beats, Class IC blockade accumulates and only partially dissipates during diastole. At 64 bpm, the diastolic interval is roughly 700 ms — far too short for a drug with a 15–20 s dissociation time to fully unbind. This basal blockade slows phase 0 conduction velocity across the working myocardium, widening the QRS on every beat regardless of rate. Faster rates make this worse (use-dependence), but the widening at rest is already a feature of Class IC kinetics, not a sign of toxicity.
Option B is incorrect: Class IC (flecainide, propafenone) leaves APD and ERP unchanged in Purkinje fibers and ventricles; the QRS widening is due to slowed phase 0 conduction velocity from Na⁺ blockade, not K⁺ channel effects on repolarization time.
Option C is incorrect: Class IC agents bind open and inactivated sodium channels, not resting-state channels preferentially; and their QRS widening occurs in structurally normal hearts — that is the flecainide indication.
Option D is incorrect: baseline QRS widening is an expected pharmacodynamic effect of Class IC drugs even at therapeutic doses and at rest; it does not indicate toxicity in isolation. Monitoring for excessive QRS prolongation (>25% increase) is part of safe use, but the degree seen here is expected.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man takes nifedipine for systolic hypertension. He develops paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia and his primary care physician considers using his existing calcium channel blocker for rate control. Which of the following BEST explains why nifedipine is not appropriate for this indication?
options: Nifedipine blocks L-type calcium channels in both vascular smooth muscle and cardiac nodal tissue equally, making its cardiac effects on the AV node unpredictable
Dihydropyridines such as nifedipine act preferentially on vascular smooth muscle and have no clinically meaningful direct effect on cardiac nodal tissue, making them ineffective as antiarrhythmics
Nifedipine is a non-selective calcium channel blocker that would produce dangerous excessive bradycardia in addition to rate control
Dihydropyridines are classified as Class IV antiarrhythmics but are reserved for hypertension because their vasodilatory side effects outweigh their antiarrhythmic benefit
questions.explanation:
Option B is correct: nifedipine is a dihydropyridine (DHP) calcium channel blocker that acts preferentially on vascular smooth muscle L-type calcium channels; DHPs are not Class IV antiarrhythmics and have no direct effect on cardiac nodal tissue conduction or refractoriness. The two major groups of calcium channel blockers differ in their tissue selectivity: DHPs (nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine) act on vascular smooth muscle to reduce blood pressure and have no meaningful effect on SA node automaticity, AV conduction velocity, or AV nodal ERP. Only the non-DHPs — verapamil and diltiazem — have prominent cardiac effects and are classified as Class IV antiarrhythmics. Rate control in SVT or atrial fibrillation requires a non-DHP; nifedipine is simply the wrong drug class for this purpose.
Option A is incorrect: DHP agents do not equally block cardiac and vascular L-type channels — their selectivity for vascular smooth muscle L-type channels over cardiac channels is the defining characteristic of the DHP class; their cardiac effects are minimal, not unpredictable.
Option C is incorrect: nifedipine is a DHP and has no clinically significant effect on the SA or AV node; it would not cause bradycardia. Bradycardia and AV block are risks of non-DHP agents (verapamil, diltiazem).
Option D is incorrect: DHPs are explicitly NOT classified as Class IV antiarrhythmics — the slide states directly that dihydropyridines “are not Class IV antiarrhythmics.” Class IV is reserved for the non-DHP agents verapamil and diltiazem.
